newsitem.title: USA: FCC chief sees antitrust barrier to an AT&T merger.
newsitem.headline: FCC chief sees antitrust barrier to an AT&T merger.

text.p: A mega-merger by AT&T Corp and SBC Communications Inc, the U.S. regional Bell, remains unthinkable in the view of most antitrust experts, Federal Communications Commission chief Reed Hundt said on Thursday.
"All of the published comments of the experts has been that it is unthinkable," Hundt said of a possible merger between the companies.

The FCC chairman said he was responding to the hypothetical merger after AT&T Chairman Robert Allen first raised the possibility in a speech Tuesday and his company mailed the speech to hundreds of Washington decision-makers in an initial effort to sway opinion in favor of such a deal.

"I didn't see anything in (Allen's) argument that would suggest that any of these experts are about to change their views," Hundt said in an interview after speaking to 700 corporate executives at a Price Waterhouse conference in New York.
"If the FCC has to decide this issue and we go to those experts to decide whether to approve such a deal, you can predict what the overwhelming weight of opinion will be," Hundt told Reuters.

To date, neither AT&T or SBC have commented on whether they are holding talks on a possible merge. Such a deal, if completed, would create a company with a stock market value of $110 billion, making it the largest corporate merger in history.

The U.S. Telecommunications Act of 1996 set forth a mechanism for doing away with legal barriers that have barred Baby Bells from entering the U.S. long-distance market since the break-up of the old AT&T telephone monopoly in 1992.
But many legal experts have argued that a merger between AT&T and SBC, the former Southwestern Bell, would defeat efforts to open U.S. telecom markets to greater competition.
In particular, they have said the combination of AT&T and SBC would create an insurmountable barrier to competition in the Baby Bell's local phone service region.
